  [OUTLINE_NUMBER_FULL] [AGENDA_ITEM_NAME]
[IGNORE_INDENT]","reportContent":null,"minutesDiscussion":"ALTERNATE MOTION

Cr Kimberly Hone
Cr Meredith Dennis (Deputy Mayor)

RESOLVED that Council urgently establishes a Hastings Point Wastewater Treatment Plant consultative committee with the following parameters:

  1. Membership to comprise of four (4) community representatives, four (4) Council staff one (1) whom is from the Sustainability and Environment Unit) and a Chair to be a representative from the NSW State Government such as Public Works or similar.

  2. Membership to exclude persons who have a conflict of interest including but not limited to adjoining land holders.

  3. Community representatives to comprise of residents from across the Tweed shire community including at least one (1) representative directly from the community in question (Hastings Point, Bogangar or Pottsville).

  4. Community representatives to be selected and approved by Council through an expression of interest process, three (3) of which with criteria that ideally demonstrates qualifications that are directly related to water and/or wastewater management, and one (1) of with financial management (CPA certified).

  5. The Terms of Reference be prepared for the committee which clarifies it's role to be focused on providing feedback to Council officers on strategic aspects of the project which will include:
    1. a startup meeting which is a briefing for the committee on the parameters of the concept design;
    2. the status of the project;
    3. the financial arrangements and funding;
    4. a summary of the proposed broader community consultation that has occurred and will occur; and 
    5. timing of the various phases.

  6. Feedback on determination of the Multicriteria Assessment criteria for the assessment of the two (2) options being considered and feedback on the draft concept designs for the two (2) options prior to finalisation and submission to Council.

  7. The timeframe of the committees first meeting to commence as soon as possible and to terminate prior to the submission of the preferred option to Council.

  8. Community consultation to proceed concurrently in accordance with Council's Community Engagement Participation Plan.

  9. Committee minutes to be reported to Council.
 

The Motion was Carried 

VOTE FOR - Cr Chris Cherry (Mayor), Cr Meredith Dennis (Deputy Mayor), Cr Rhiannon Brinsmead, Cr Reece Byrnes, Cr Nola Firth, Cr Kimberly Hone, Cr James Owen
VOTE AGAINST - None
ABSENT. DID NOT VOTE - None

Cr Reece Byrnes left the meeting at 05:07pm.

RESUMPTION OF STANDING ORDERS

Cr Rhiannon Brinsmead
Cr Meredith Dennis (Deputy Mayor)
 
RESOLVED that Standing Orders be resumed.

The Motion was Carried

VOTE FOR - Cr Chris Cherry (Mayor), Cr Meredith Dennis (Deputy Mayor), Cr Rhiannon Brinsmead, Cr Nola Firth, Cr Kimberly Hone, Cr James Owen
VOTE AGAINST - None
ABSENT. DID NOT VOTE - Cr Reece Byrnes

  [OUTLINE_NUMBER_FULL] [AGENDA_ITEM_NAME]
[IGNORE_INDENT]","reportContent":null,"minutesDiscussion":"Cr Rhiannon Brinsmead
Cr Meredith Dennis (Deputy Mayor)

RESOLVED that:

  1. The Minutes of the Floodplain Management Advisory Committee Meeting held Friday 28 March 2025 be received. These minutes will become confirmed at the next scheduled Floodplain Management Advisory Committee Meeting to be held in June/July 2025.

  2. The Executive Leadership Team's recommendations be adopted as follows: 

a) Flood assessment of Pacific Motorway
That Council:
(i) should expedite work on the Tweed Valley Floodplain Risk Management Study as well as related changes to Planning Instruments to prevent further cumulative impacts of development on the Floodplain, including options for future modifications to the Pacific Motorway.

(ii) responds to TfNSW’s letter, by requesting that any planning associated with the potential raising of the M1 must ensure that no additional impediment is provided to flow of flood water across the floodplain and preferably would also include measures to redress impediments provided by the existing M1 construction.

b) Drainage Reset Program
That Council and other relevant agencies urge the NSW Government, alongside NEMA, and the Reconstruction Authority, to collaborate in establishing a dedicated, indexed funding program for ongoing drainage maintenance and critical infrastructure upgrades. This program must extend beyond sediment clearing to include the modernisation of floodgates, culverts, and other essential drainage assets. Without this commitment, past investments will be undermined, and flood-prone communities will remain at risk. The investment required for regular maintenance is far more cost-effective than disaster recovery, and we will encourage all levels of government to come together in securing long-term flood resilience for the Northern Rivers. 

c) Flood Planning Levels
That Council Officers submit a report to Council proposing an Interim Flood Planning Levels Policy, and parallel updates to DCP-A3 Development of Flood Liable Land, based upon a Defined Flood Event consisting of the highest (worst case) of the following: 

  • Tweed Valley Flood Study 2009 and Tweed Coastal Creeks 2010 1% AEP (100 Year ARI) level (Old DFE) 
  • The historic Flood of Record peak level (eg: 2022, 2017, 1954) 
  • To make reasonable allowance for Climate Change, the Tweed Valley Flood Study Update and Expansion 2024 0.2% AEP (500 Yr ARI) level and the Tweed Coastal Creeks Flood Study 2010 0.2% AEP (500 Yr ARI) level with a minimum of 2.9m AHD applied to coastal areas to reflect contemporary sea level rise projections 
  • Apply a freeboard of 0.5m to all Defined Flood Event levels to reach Flood Planning Level (Minimum Habitable Floor Level) 
  • Replace the 0.2% AEP (500 Yr ARI) layers with contemporary 1% AEP Climate Change scenarios when investigated in future Flood Risk Management Studies using the most recent science and government guidance.

d) High Flow Areas
That Council Officers submit a report to Council proposing an Interim Flood Planning Levels Policy, and parallel updates to DCP-A3 - Development of Flood Liable Land, including adoption of a “High Flow Area” based upon: 

  • In the Tweed Valley catchment, the Tweed Valley Flood Study Update and Expansion 2024 1% AEP ‘’Depth-Velocity Product” threshold of 0.4m2/s 
  • In the Tweed Coastal Creeks catchments, maintain the current High Flow Area mapping which is based on a 1% AEP “Depth-Velocity Product” threshold of 0.3m2/s 
  • Revisit the definition of “High Flow Area” planning controls in future Flood Risk Management Studies and Plans and re-establish robust, consistent, shire-wide, parameters for inclusion in future updates to planning policies.

The Motion was Carried 

VOTE FOR - Cr Chris Cherry (Mayor), Cr Meredith Dennis (Deputy Mayor), Cr Rhiannon Brinsmead, Cr Nola Firth, Cr James Owen
VOTE AGAINST - None
ABSENT. DID NOT VOTE - Cr Reece Byrnes, Cr Kimberly Hone

  [OUTLINE_NUMBER_FULL] [AGENDA_ITEM_NAME]
[IGNORE_INDENT]","reportContent":null,"minutesDiscussion":"AMENDMENT

Cr Rhiannon Brinsmead
Cr Kimberly Hone

RESOLVED that Council:

  1. Receives the Minutes of the Local Traffic Committee Meeting held Thursday 8 May 2025; and 

  2. The Executive Leadership Team's recommendations be adopted as follows:

6.1.   Tweed Valley Way and Clothiers Creek Road, intersection
Transport for NSW shared the most recent 5-year crash data for the intersection. The most prevalent crash type was Road User Movement Code 10 being vehicles approaching the intersection on Clothiers Creek Road not giving way to southbound traffic on Tweed Valley Way. The initial review by TfNSW was that improved approach signage and linemarking may increase usability of the intersection and a speed limit reduction was not warranted. The Committee members were in concurrence that TfNSW should reconsider extending the 60km/h limit from the south and remove the current 80km/h limit, which is less than the minimum length recommend in the Speed Zoning Standard.

7.1. Sutherland Street, Kingscliff
To improve sight distance for drivers entering Sutherland Street from Viking Street, Kingscliff, a 20m length of yellow no stopping line be installed on the north-west side of Sutherland Street extending from Viking Street.

7.2. Florence Street, Tweed Heads
The request for prohibitive parking to be placed between the driveways of 6 to 10 Florence Street, Tweed Heads is not supported. Vehicles parking in this location are not breaching road rules, and the current configuration of the intersection creates no potential conflict points.

7.3. LATE ITEM McPhail Avenue, Kingscliff
The request to remove the existing bus stop on McPhail Avenue, Kingscliff adjacent to 58 Cudgen Road was not supported given that:

  • there is a current high demand for that location
  • there are adjacent pedestrian facilities
  • the stop is on a commercial bus route that is unlikely to be changed
  • there is no suitable stop within close proximity, and
  • removing the J pole would not prevent bus users hailing the bus at that location.
  1. Writes to Kingscliff High School:

    1. requesting that it approaches Transport for NSW requesting the 601 bus route to include a new bus stop at the school.
    2. communicate with students and parents reminding them of safety crossing roads when travelling to bus stops and their behaviour at bus stops particularly those that are adjacent to people's homes.
 

The Motion was Carried 

VOTE FOR - Cr Chris Cherry (Mayor), Cr Meredith Dennis (Deputy Mayor), Cr Rhiannon Brinsmead, Cr Reece Byrnes, Cr Nola Firth, Cr Kimberly Hone, Cr James Owen
VOTE AGAINST - None
ABSENT. DID NOT VOTE - None

Cr Kimberly Hone

RESOLVED that the Mayor writes to the Victorian Government:
 
  1. condemning the use of aerial culling for koalas. This method is not supported as a humane method of euthanasia because it does not allow appropriate prior assessment of the condition of the animal, does not allow for verification of the absence of joeys in pouch and the animals cannot be assessed as to whether they were euthanised effectively 

  2. urging for the relocation of koalas as a preferred method of population management

  3. noting that culling undermines the intended welfare purpose of the koalas to the extent that this practice should not be used

  4. acknowledges koalas are a national icon and should be protected.
 
The Motion was Carried 

VOTE FOR - Cr Chris Cherry (Mayor), Cr Meredith Dennis (Deputy Mayor), Cr Rhiannon Brinsmead, Cr Nola Firth, Cr Kimberly Hone, Cr James Owen
VOTE AGAINST - None
ABSENT. DID NOT VOTE - Cr Reece Byrnes

  [OUTLINE_NUMBER_FULL] [AGENDA_ITEM_NAME]
[IGNORE_INDENT]","reportContent":null,"minutesDiscussion":"Councillor Brinsmead asks what has been done / can be done to address the debris, the erosion, and the dune recession?

The Director Sustainable Communities and Environment replied:
Through you Madam Mayor, The Tweed Shire coastline is experiencing its worst erosion in decades. Ex-Tropical Cyclone Alfred severely weakened the beaches, and two months of large swells, high tides, and tidal anomalies have worsened the situation. Erosion has reached the tertiary dune, causing large trees to fall onto the beach and creating safety hazards from 4-metre-high erosion scarps.
 
Council’s efforts to date have focused on maintaining public safety where access is available. The first actions included removal of fallen and hanging trees along all beach accesses.
 
Beach access infrastructure and dunes have been heavily damaged. Unfortunately, State and Federal funding did not cover post-cyclone cleanup, limiting Council’s ability to undertake safety and restoration works. High tides and a reduced beach profile allow minimal space to operate safely.
 
Current work is limited to essential safety measures - pushing fallen trees back and clearing emergency and pedestrian access points where possible. Pushing down dune scarps to create access points causes more erosion when the beach is still in an erosive phase.  Debris removal is ongoing but challenged by continued erosion and high tides bringing new debris. Some beach access paths remain closed for public safety and dune protection. These are reassessed weekly and will be reopened as the beach is rebuilding. 
 
Approaches have also been made to the Minister for Recovery and other agencies for assistance.  Specifically, staff are advocating for:
 
  • Support to reinstate key pedestrian and emergency beach vehicle accesses
  • Funding and equipment to remove or reposition large debris for long-term dune repair
  • Advice from NSW Soil Conservation Services on managing this Crown land responsibly 
  • Help with community messaging about the scale of damage and current limitations.
 
Council will continue efforts to manage hazards and maintain public safety as conditions allow.

[IGNORE_INDENT]","reportContent":null,"minutesDiscussion":"Councillor Brinsmead asks what can be done to better meet community expectations with respect to vegetation maintenance (roadside and ‘other’) and weed management?

The Director Sustainable Communities and Environment replied:
Through you Madam Mayor, Vegetation maintenance service levels are set each year by Council through the endorsement of Council’s Delivery Program, Operational Plan and budget.  Should Council be inclined to increase its service level in this area, it would require a reduction in service levels of an alternate program, alternatively, a special rate variation to increase the budget. 
 
Notwithstanding, given that weed management is currently funded and carried out by various Council services and external agencies such as Rous County Council, it would be both strategically and financially prudent for Council to allocate resources toward a comprehensive strategic review of its weed management approach. This would ensure informed decision-making, rather than committing additional funding without a clear understanding of the potential impacts or limitations of the current approach.


","isPublic":false,"isPublished":false,"isCurrentItem":false,"meeting":null,"reports":[{"id":22264,"name":"Question With Notice","isUploaded":0,"reportTemplateId":18,"wordTemplateId":8,"pdfMediaFullPath":"stream/TWEED/tmp_fa2e923413.pdf","token":"56e4b531-0394-43e4-9548-8bfad421faa2","isPublic":false}],"attachments":[],"actionSheets":[],"bookmarks":[{"id":3252,"name":"36","eventId":1648,"title":"QWN - Cr Brinsmead - Vegetation Maintenance ","text":"QWN - Cr Brinsmead - Vegetation Maintenance ","startTime":14490,"duration":null,"itemId":28107,"sortOrder":37,"minutesSortOrder":37,"parentId":-1,"additionalParentId":-1}],"minutes":[]},{"id":28108,"name":"QWN - Cr Brinsmead - DA Processing Times","parentId":27026,"sortOrder":62,"minutesSortOrder":67,"minutesParentId":27026,"outlineNumber":"3","fullOutlineNumber":"20.3.","htmlContent":"
  [OUTLINE_NUMBER_FULL] [AGENDA_ITEM_NAME]
[IGNORE_INDENT]","reportContent":null,"minutesDiscussion":"Cr Brinsmead - DA Processing Times – Councillor Brinsmead asks can we please have an update on the current DA processing time in the Tweed Shire?

The General Manager replied:
Thank you for the question Councillor. I take this opportunity to thank all councillors for their encouragement in our council improving its assessment performance. Respectful of everyone’s time, whilst also being very cognisant of the interest in this matter by the State, proponents, councillors and members of the community, I will be providing you a brief response tonight but tabling and providing you all a more detailed response in hard copy that will also sit on the public record and Minutes.

As of May 2025, Tweed Shire Council has made strong, measurable progress in improving Development Application processing times and reducing the number of undetermined applications in our system. At its peak in late 2023, the number of undetermined DAs exceeded 500. Today, we’ve reduced that to 178 - a 64% reduction - and we are well on track to stabilise at a more sustainable caseload of around 150.

We are also processing applications faster. In May, we determined 95 DAs with an average assessment time of 126 days and a median time of 82 days. So far in June, the average has dropped further to 113 days. The median time - a more accurate reflection of performance for councils with outlier DAs - was 94 days across the financial year to May, below the State target of 115.

This turnaround is thanks to a whole-of-Council approach, involving planning, engineering, building, and environmental teams, and supported by Councillors through past resourcing decisions, including the special rate variation and funding through general rate revenue for additional staff in the 2025/26 budget.

We’re also maintaining quality: of the 652 DAs processed this financial year, 81% have been approved, showing we’re not only faster - we’re delivering good planning outcomes.

However, unless the cumulative tally used in the Department’s DA League Table is reset on 1 July 2025, Tweed will remain burdened by past statistics and outliers, despite the real improvements now being delivered.

If the current cumulative tally continues and if the average only is reported, Tweed will remain burdened by past statistics and outliers, despite our improved current performance.

Thank you.

Detailed Response
As of May 2025, Tweed Shire Council has made significant progress in improving Development Application processing times in response to the NSW Government’s Statement of Expectations Order, and importantly in reducing the number of undetermined DAs in our system.

At its peak in late 2023, our undetermined DAs exceeded 500. Through a focused, whole-of-Council effort, we’ve reduced that number to 178 by mid-June 2025 - a 64% reduction - and we are now tracking toward a more sustainable caseload of around 150 applications.

The cumulative average or mean assessment time across the year to May 2025 is currently 149 days. Comparatively, if the statistics used the median rather than the mean or average, Council’s year-to-date median assessment time from July 2024 to May 2025 would be just 94 days - which is comfortably below the State’s target of 115 days.

This more accurately reflects the performance of the revised and streamlined assessment processes now in place. The mean or average is sensitive to extreme values (outliers), while the median provides a better measure of central tendency when the data is skewed. The mean/average and median are both measures of central tendency in statistics, but they are calculated differently and serve different purposes. Mathematically, it is best to use the mean/ average to describe the centre of a dataset when the distribution is mostly symmetrical and there are no outliers. It is best to use the median when the distribution is either skewed or there are outliers present. These differences highlight the importance of choosing the appropriate measure based on the data characteristics. This is important to note when reading the Department’s DA League Table as it only currently reports Mean/ Average. It therefore does not provide an accurate representation of central tendency for growth councils such as Tweed that might be dealing with DAs for large greenfield developments and normal residential dwellings. The time to assess a large complex subdivision will invariably take longer than assessment of a house or pergola. Thus, mean or average is a better reflection for councils who predominantly assess routine DAs whereas median is a better representation for councils such as Tweed, Central Coast, Blacktown, Ballina, Liverpool, Sutherland, The Hills, Queenbeyan-Palerang, etc that will be dealing with outlier DAs that skew the statistical mean / average.

Whilst the average / mean assessment of a council may suit some narratives, it is not reflective nor transparent of all councils DA assessment performance. By way of example, Council A may assess 3 House DAs with respective assessment times of 60, 70 and 80 days providing an average of 70 days, whilst Council B may assess 3 similar house DAs with assessment times of 30, 40 and 50 days plus a single DA of a moveable dwelling park comprising 93 sites which took 210 days to assess and a 200 lot subdivision in a sensitive environmental area subject to bush fire hazard in 310 days which provides an average assessment time of 128 days.

By comparison, the median assessment time for Council A would be 70 days, the same as its average while the median assessment for Council B, with the outliers, would be 50 days. This example demonstrates why the median can be a better reflection of performance when trying to ascertain whether councils are delivering on housing outcomes.  In this example, Council B is quicker in assessing housing DAs and is also dealing with more complex matters that result in greater housing outcomes. For these reasons the DA League table is statistically flawed in only reporting averages and is not transparent in truly comparing the diverse range of 128 councils dealing with varying complexities and types of DA matters.

I am of the view that if the Department engaged an expert statistician, mathematician or actuary, they would be advised that the use of median in the DA League Table would provide the Minister a more reliable and accurate view of a council’s measure of central data tendency with respect to DA performance, given the varying levels of complexities in DAs submitted.

An everyday example that councillors and members of the community may be familiar with where median is typically used over mean or average to provide a more accurate representation of market conditions is in relation to real estate pricing where the median house price is reported for cities, suburbs or states. This is to avoid outliers distorting and inflating the actual central market price for homes in a region. For example, when reporting prices in Sydney median is used so outlier suburbs like Vaucluse do not distort the figure as that suburbs pricing is not representative of the broader pricing of homes across the Sydney basin. Similarly, this applies when reporting DA assessment times due to outlier complex DA’s that some councils may be dealing with.

In May alone, Council determined 95 DAs with an average or mean processing time of 126 days and a median assessment time of 82 days. And so far in June, staff have finalised 30 DAs with an average or mean of 113 days for the month - sitting below the current expectation order benchmark and a median time of 100 days indicating we are getting through the outlier DAs as both the mean/average and median gap closes. These are clear indicators of consistent improvement.

Tweed has always focused strongly on working with applicants to achieve good planning outcomes. While the State’s Order rightly seeks efficiency, it is heavily weighted toward determination speed, rather than planning quality or results that achieve an approved development. Council continues to maintain rigorous assessments, with an approval rate of 81% for the 24/25 financial year based on 652 applications. These statistics underscore our commitment to enabling appropriate, high-quality development.

In the past, Council has supported additional resource via a special rate variation and to further support the DA priority Council has allocated additional funding in the 2025/26 Budget for new planning and technical staff, commencing 1 July. However, I must note that this resourcing will be funded from rate revenue, meaning ratepayers are effectively subsidising new development. Council’s Executive will continue to advocate for statutory DA fees to better reflect the real costs involved in DA assessment. I thank Councillors for endorsing these initiatives as they have and will be crucial to meeting the Expectation Order into the future.

Staff have worked incredibly hard and taken a whole-of-Council approach that has underpinned this improvement - involving not only planning, but also engineering, building, environmental health, and ecology teams. It has truly been a collective effort. But I take this opportunity to highlight the tireless effort of our Director Planning & Regulation, Denise Galle who I have witnessed first-hand work tirelessly since first assuming the position of Manager Building and Environmental Health and then the Director Planning & Regulation role to facilitate positive development and environmental outcomes whilst significantly reducing not only our outstanding number of DAs in the system, but the average assessment time.

Looking ahead, we are confident that lodgement and assessment times will continue to improve. However, the speed at which we meet the State’s expectations will depend on whether the NSW Government re-sets the League Table from 1 July 2025. And for the reasons expressed above, we believe the DA League table should also report Median assessment times to provide the Minister and the community greater visibility of how individual councils are working collaboratively with the State to address the housing crisis.

If the current cumulative tally continues and if the average only is reported, Tweed will remain burdened by past statistics and outliers, despite our improved current performance. Importantly, for the Ministers consideration, is that councils whose performance decreases would not be immediately reflective unless the League Table is reset at 1 July. It is for these reasons we believe the Department must ensure that results shown, reflect current performance whilst retaining a historical record to assess performance over time.

Finally, staff have prepared an operational report for the NSW Department of Planning, Housing and Infrastructure, outlining the actions already undertaken and an implementation plan for 2025/26. I also take this opportunity to inform councillors that I have formally invited the Department to undertake a peer review of this work, and we would welcome constructive feedback on our progress and path forward.

[IGNORE_INDENT]","reportContent":null,"minutesDiscussion":"Councillor Owen asks what options are there to address the drainage issues that cause flooding at the Kingscliff Regional Sports Complex, particularly from the drain on the eastern boundary?

The Director Sustainable Communities and Environment replied:
Through you Madam Mayor, Despite the sand-based profile, the combination of high rainfall through summer into winter has caused ongoing usability and maintenance issues at Walter Peate sportsfield. Stormwater runoff from the properties along Murphys Road are affecting the southern end of the main field.  Staff are exploring the following options to resolve the issue: 
 
  • Redirection of the stormwater to the southern training fields
  • Full redirection of the piped system to the existing stormwater network in Wommin Bay Road to remove the ‘minor’ storm event flows from the fields, and
  • Improving and lengthening the concrete dish drain to run more water to the south.
 
However, prior to committing to an option a survey will need to be undertaken to assess the impacts and costs of the proposed the identified outlet locations.

[IGNORE_INDENT]","reportContent":null,"minutesDiscussion":"Councillor Owen asks, how much has Council spent on external consultants in the current and previous three (3) financial years?

The Director Corporate Services replied:
The definition of ‘consultant’ can be challenging to define and to differentiate between the various tasks undertaken by our suppliers, however staff have used a number of accounting codes to attempt to gather the requested information noting there is no particular statutory requirement to present these amounts in our annual financial reporting.

In 21/22 the expenditure on external consultants was $750,674 - noting that $447,753 of that amount was for the new Works Depot and Clarrie Hall Dam - the $750,674 represents 0.29% of the 21/22 financial year budget.

In 22/23 the expenditure on external consultants was $1,486,896 - noting that $892,786 of that amount was for the new Works Depot, Clarrie Hall Dam and the Growth Management Housing Strategy. The $1,486,896 represents 0.59% of the 22/23 financial year budget.

In 23/24 the expenditure on external consultants was $1,847,050 - noting that $1,084,042 of that amount was for the Hastings Point Sewerage Treatment Plant, Phase 1 of the implementation and data migration of Councils Technology One corporate IT system, Clarrie Hall Dam and the Growth Management Housing Strategy. The $1,847,050 represents 0.64% of the 23/24 financial year budget.

The 24/25 year to date expenditure on external consultants is $1,527,240 - noting that $724,212 of that amount was for Phase 1 and Phase 2 of the implementation and data migration of Councils Technology One corporate IT system and the Growth Management Housing Strategy. The $1,527,240 represents 0.54% of the budget.

[IGNORE_INDENT]","reportContent":null,"minutesDiscussion":"Councillor Owen asks what business continuity measures can be implemented to enhance the assessment and determination processes of construction and occupation certificates to improve outcomes and timelines, ensuring the determination process continues seamlessly when staff members are on leave, so applicants do not experience financial impact of delays?

The Director Planning and Regulation replied:
Thank you, Councillor Owen. This is a timely question, especially with current housing supply pressures and the Department of Planning’s focus on fast-tracking approvals. While performance targets often focus on Development Applications, certificate approvals are equally vital to delivering new housing.

Tweed Shire Council has systems in place to support continuity. For Occupation Certificates, inspections are booked centrally and not tied to any one officer. This means the first available registered certifier can be assigned, helping avoid delays when staff are away.

For Construction Certificates, while the assessment is more complex, Council is the certifier - not an individual - so any accredited Building Surveyor with the appropriate level can assess or determine a certificate. This provides internal flexibility, especially for Class 1 buildings.

For higher-class buildings, reassignment is more limited due to fewer staff holding unrestricted accreditation. 

Like many NSW councils, we are seeing a decline in these accreditations, which may require us to engage external certifiers in future - at a significant cost.

In short, Council has measures in place to minimise disruption, but resourcing and accreditation constraints remain a challenge we continue to monitor closely.

Cr Kimberly Hone
Cr Rhiannon Brinsmead

RESOLVED that:
 
  1. Development Application DA24/0450 for the use of existing buildings as farm stay accommodation at Lot 4 DP 565754, No. 396 Melaleuca Road, Cudgen be refused for the following reasons:
     
    1. Pursuant to Section 4.15(1)(a)(i) of the Environmental Planning and Assessment Act 1979, the consent authority is not satisfied the proposal is not inconsistent with the aim of the Tweed Local Environmental Plan 2014 as set out in Clause 1.2(2)(b) to encourage a sustainable local economy and small business, employment, agriculture, affordable housing, recreational, arts, social, cultural, tourism and sustainable industry opportunities appropriate to Tweed. The application which seeks approval for farm stay accommodation on agricultural land does not satisfactorily demonstrate that it meets the requirements to be defined as farm stay accommodation. It is therefore prohibited tourist and visitor accommodation in a rural zone and is not considered an appropriate tourist opportunity for the agricultural land.
    2. Pursuant to Section 4.15(1)(a)(i) of the Environmental Planning and Assessment Act 1979, the consent authority is not satisfied that the proposal is for a permissible purpose of development in the RU1 Primary Production zone under the Tweed Local Environmental Plan 2014. The consent authority is not satisfied the proposed farm stay accommodation is ancillary to the commercial farm as required by the definition of farm stay accommodation.
    3. Pursuant to Section 4.15(1)(a)(i) of the Environmental Planning and Assessment Act 1979, the consent authority is not satisfied the proposal is not inconsistent with the objectives of the RU1 Primary Production zone pursuant to Clause 2.3(2) of the Tweed Local Environmental Plan 2014. The consent authority is not satisfied the proposed tourist and visitor accommodation is ancillary to an agricultural use of the land, and would not impact upon the agricultural viability of the site.
    4. Pursuant to Section 4.15(1)(e) of the Environmental Planning and Assessment Act 1979, for the reasons set out in the preceding reasons, the application is not in the public interest.

  2. ATTACHMENT 3 is CONFIDENTIAL in accordance with Section 10A(2) of the Local Government Act 1993, because it contains:

    (e)     information that would, if disclosed, prejudice the maintenance of law

     

 
The Amendment was Carried 

VOTE FOR - Cr Chris Cherry (Mayor), Cr Meredith Dennis (Deputy Mayor), Cr Rhiannon Brinsmead, Cr Nola Firth, Cr Kimberly Hone, Cr James Owen
VOTE AGAINST - None
ABSENT. DID NOT VOTE - Cr Reece Byrnes

AMENDMENT BECOMING THE MOTION

The Amendment on becoming the motion was Carried

VOTE FOR - Cr Chris Cherry (Mayor), Cr Meredith Dennis (Deputy Mayor), Cr Rhiannon Brinsmead, Cr Nola Firth, Cr James Owen
VOTE AGAINST - Cr Kimberly Hone
ABSENT. DID NOT VOTE - Cr Reece Byrnes

32      Detailed Landscaping Plan – Native species
Prior to the issue of a Construction Certificate the landscaping plan shall be revised and submitted for review to the satisfaction of Council's General Manager or delegate. The detailed plan of landscaping shall meet the following plant selection criteria:
  1. A minimum of 80% local native species to the Tweed Shire and maximum of 20% non-locally occurring Australian native species to apply to all trees.
  2. A minimum of 80% local native species to the Tweed Shire and maximum of 20% Australian native or exotic species to apply to other plants (shrubs, ground cover and similar).
  3. No declared weed species listed under the NSW Biosecurity Act 2016 (or as amended).
  4. The landscape plan is to identify the planting of one small tree in the DSZ in each strata lot with a minimum height of 5m at maturity. 
  5. Trees are to be minimum 45L pot size. 
  6. Locally-occurring native species are to comprise appropriate species selected from the Tweed Shire Native Species Planting Guide available online at:
     <www.tweed.nsw.gov.au/environment/native-plants-wildlife/native-plants>

The meeting opened with a Prayer read by Pastor Tara Jones from The Gathering, Tweed Heads. 

I am going to pray in the Christian tradition today and I invite you to join me or take a moment for reflection.
 
Heavenly Father,


We come before You today with hearts humbled by the responsibility of leadership and governance. We acknowledge You as the ultimate source of wisdom, justice, and truth.


Lord, we thank You for the beauty and richness of the Tweed Shire — for its rivers, mountains, coastline, and the people who call this region home. 


As this council gathers to make decisions that shape the future of our community, we ask that You would pour out Your wisdom — not the wisdom of man, but the kind that is pure, peace-loving, considerate, full of mercy and good fruit, impartial and sincere.


Grant each councillor around this table the grace to lead with integrity, courage, and humility. Help them to listen deeply, speak wisely, and act justly — always with compassion for the people they serve.


Lord, we lift up the younger generations who call this shire their home. May they be blessed with opportunity, inspired by vision, and protected by wise decisions made on their behalf today. May this council lead in such a way that future generations will thrive — spiritually, socially, and economically.


Strengthen every leader here for the tasks ahead. Give them clarity in times of confusion, unity in times of division, and boldness in times when hard decisions must be made. I ask for your love and protection to wash over each councillor and their families


We commit this meeting and this council to Your care. May Your peace rest upon this place, and may Your purposes be fulfilled in this region for generations to come.


In Jesus’ name we pray,


Amen.

RESOLVED that:

  1. The Minutes of the Local Traffic Committee Meeting held Thursday 12 June 2025 be received.

  2. The Local Traffic Committee Recommendations be adopted as follows: 
6.1.    Couchy Creek Road, Numinbah 
That the requests for additional signage on Couchy Creek Road are not supported. Given the infrequent demand outside of peak periods and since it's a public road, signage for ‘Local Traffic Only’ and additional speed advisory signs are not likely to be effective. Increasing prohibitive parking would be challenging given enforcement capacity. Residents are encouraged to report illegal parking to Rangers. The submission made by the resident will be shared with National Parks and Wildlife Services for further investigation and consideration of additional barriers to protect the natural environment. 

7.1.    Peninsula Drive, Bilambil Heights
That resident input be sought before installation of ‘No stopping’ signage (limited to times when the school bus is in the area) in Bilambil Heights between 140-148 Peninsula Drive and 160-162 Peninsula Drive, Bilambil Heights, and 15 metres from the intersection when entering into Broadwater Esplanade. 

7.2.    Recreation Street, Tweed Heads
The existing 'No parking police vehicles excepted’ signage on Recreation Street, Tweed Heads, in front of the old police station, be relocated to in front of the courthouse.

7.3.    Ourimbah Road, Tweed Heads
That the request to improve and reinforce prohibitive parking be supported on Ourimbah Road, Tweed Heads, being that:
  • The existing ‘No parking’ signage on both sides of the curve adjacent to Kinetic Bus Lines entrance, be upgraded to yellow no stopping line marking. 
  • The existing ‘No parking’ signage on the inside of the curve adjacent to 25 Ourimbah Road, be changed to yellow no stopping line marking.
  • The existing ‘No parking’ signage on the north side of Ourimbah Road at the intersection of Ducat Street, be upgraded to yellow no stopping line marking.
  • The yellow no stopping line be installed on the south side of Ourimbah Road from Ducat Street, to the new driveway at number 1-9 Ourimbah Road (approximately 20 metres in length).

7.4.    Sutherland Street, Kingscliff
That:
1. The installation of a marked crossing and/or children's crossing on Sutherland Street, Kingscliff adjacent to Kingscliff Primary School is not supported as:
  • The proposed location does not meet the minimal pedestrian warrants.
  • The crossing would encourage parents to park on Sutherland Street when the pick-up/drop-off area is on Orient Street.
  • There are pedestrian facilities (refuges) in close proximity.
2. The disused Children's Crossing on Orient Street near Sutherland Street, Kingscliff, be removed subject to confirmation from the Kingscliff Primary School.
3. Further investigation for upgrades including converting the existing refuges to a Children’s Crossing be investigated and this matter is to be a 'business arising' on the 10 July 2025 LTC meeting

7.5.    Intersection Minjungbal Drive and William Street, Tweed Heads South 
The installation of yellow no stopping lines around the intersection of Minjungbal Drive and William Street, Tweed Heads South, to reinforce the existing road rules is not supported as:
•    Yellow no stopping lines and signage do not guarantee compliance.
•    Installing yellow lines are an ongoing cost for maintenance and can be impacted by debris.
•    The two recorded crashes at this intersection in the last five years are not indicative of the crash risk raised by the customer.
•    It has been reported that the offending vehicles are associated with an adjacent business and not a regular occurrence. 
•    William Street is 9m wide allowing vehicles to be parked with an ability to pass an oncoming vehicle. 
•    Minjungbal Drive has a parking lane and a continuity line over William Street which allows drivers to edge forward into Minjungbal Drive.

The Motion was Carried 

VOTE FOR - Cr Chris Cherry (Mayor), Cr Meredith Dennis (Deputy Mayor), Cr Rhiannon Brinsmead, Cr Reece Byrnes, Cr Nola Firth, Cr James Owen
VOTE AGAINST - None

AMENDMENT 1

Cr Kimberly Hone
Cr Rhiannon Brinsmead

PROPOSED that Council writes to the NSW Reconstruction Authority to provide a similar betterment prioritisation tool to that provided by Queensland Reconstruction Authority.

The Motion was Lost on the casting vote of the Mayor

VOTE FOR - Cr Rhiannon Brinsmead, Cr Kimberly Hone, Cr James Owen
VOTE AGAINST - Cr Chris Cherry (Mayor), Cr Meredith Dennis (Deputy Mayor), Cr Nola Firth
ABSENT. DID NOT VOTE - Cr Reece Byrnes


Cr Chris Cherry (Mayor)

RESOLVED that Council writes:

1. to the NSW Reconstruction Authority to provide a similar betterment prioritisation tool to that provided by Queensland Reconstruction Authority; and
2. to the Northern Rivers Joint Organisation requesting they advocate to the NSW Reconstruction Authority to provide a similar betterment prioritisation tool to that provided by Queensland Reconstruction Authority. 

The Motion was Carried 

VOTE FOR - Cr Chris Cherry (Mayor), Cr Meredith Dennis (Deputy Mayor), Cr Rhiannon Brinsmead, Cr Nola Firth, Cr Kimberly Hone, Cr James Owen

The meeting opened with a Prayer read by Reverend Michael Boyd from the Presbyterian Church, Tweed Heads 

"Gracious God, 
 
We’d prefer not to be experts in resilience.  But we recognise the good that has come; that we benefit from a wealth of expertise in our Council that strengthens our community and helps other Local Government Areas prepare for the future.
 
We pray for those who continue to bear the personal cost of those disasters, for healing and relief.
 
Even in the busyness of today, perhaps our minds are already turning to summer and wondering what might come.  Grant peace to worried minds.  Grant rest to tired bodies.  In your mercy spare us this summer.  But come what may, continue to prepare us so that our community remains safe.  Thank you for your invitation to cast all our anxiety on to you because you care for us.
 
We pray this in the name of Jesus, Amen."

I will be praying in the Christian tradition today as I am a Christian priest. I invite you to join me in prayer, or to send ‘good vibes or positive thoughts’, or just sit in silence, or to take this time as a moment of reflection.

Gracious and loving God,

Thank you for who we are, for all we have and for all we share together in this beautiful part of the world -Tweed Shire communities. We ask your blessing upon the Mayor, the Councillors, the General Manager, and all staff of Tweed Shire Council as they gather today. Grant them calm minds, clear judgment, and discerning hearts, that their decisions may be wise, just, and for the common good of all in our community.

Look kindly upon the people of the Tweed. May we work together as builders of justice and makers of peace. May our community be strengthened in prosperity and fairness, guided by compassion, tenderness, and truth. Enable us to show our true civilization in the way we care for those who are poor, marginalised, and powerless. Protect us from all evil and grant us your peace in our days.

May we all be well, happy, and healthy, and may we live with great fullness, so that each one may have what they need to flourish.

ALTERNATE MOTION

Cr Nola Firth
Cr Chris Cherry (Mayor)

RESOLVED that Council submits the following motions to the 2025 Local Government NSW (LGNSW) Annual Conference:

Motion 1 - Crown land license agreements for minor infrastructure

That LGNSW calls on the NSW Government to:
  • issuing an ‘umbrella’ licence to local government for minor infrastructure.
  • providing a full rebate to local government for minor infrastructure that Council provides to the public at no charge (i.e. not just a rebate down to the statutory minimum rental).
  • providing an automatic process for local government to obtain the rebate (i.e. not requiring an administratively heavy application process).
  • relaxing the requirement for Council to acquire land or easements for public infrastructure located on Council-manage Crown land.
Background information
Council is facing increasing financial and administrative challenges due to changes in how Crown Lands manages licensing for minor infrastructure. Previously, Council benefited from an umbrella licence that covered multiple public assets under a single, low-cost agreement. Since Crown Lands ceased this practice around 2020, each infrastructure item now incurs an individual annual licence fee, resulting in a tenfold increase in costs. This has placed significant pressure on the Waterways Program Budget, which remains fixed at $25,000 annually and is now insufficient to absorb the growing expenses.

In addition to rising costs, Council’s efforts to secure rental rebates for infrastructure provided free to the public have been largely unsuccessful. Although the Crown Lands financial concessions policy allows for rebates, they cannot reduce fees below the statutory minimum, and applications such as for the Jetty Umbrella Licence have been rejected despite the infrastructure serving the general community. The administrative burden of preparing rebate applications for each rental determination further strains Council resources, with no guarantee of success.

Compounding these issues, Crown Lands and utility providers are increasingly requiring Council to acquire easements or land for long-standing infrastructure within Council-managed Crown reserves. This includes assets like water meters and streetlighting that have existed for decades. The cost of these acquisitions is substantial, especially given the high market value of land on the East Coast. To alleviate these pressures, LGNSW should call on the NSW Government to reinstate umbrella licences, offer full rental rebates for community infrastructure, streamline the rebate process, and relaxing easement acquisition requirements.

Motion 2 - Developer Contributions

That LGNSW calls on the NSW Government to:
  • A one-off increase to the developer contributions cap to take into account CPI increases since the cap introduction in 2012.
  • Annual index the developer contributions cap.
Background information
Contributions from developers for services and infrastructure were capped in August 2012 ($20,000 per each dwelling brownfield development, $30,000 green field development) without regard to Council’s costs in providing those services and infrastructure.

It is widely known and accepted that capital costs and materials, land etc. has increased significantly since August 2012. The average lot in Tweed ten years ago sold for approximately $300,000 with developer contributions at $30,000 representing ten per cent of the land value. Today lots are in excess of $750,000 and contributions are still at $30,000 (four per cent). The former State Government was of the belief that by restricting contributions payable to councils, it will open up supply and make land more affordable. If councils cannot forward plan and build infrastructure because they cannot fund it, they simply won’t. In the longer term this will result in the necessary infrastructure for development not being available which will lead to a significant housing crisis with long lead times to resolve. Now is the time for these caps to be lifted and indexed annually to avert a crisis for the next generation.

Motion 3 – Funding for post-disaster weed management
That LGNSW calls on the NSW and Commonwealth governments to:
  • Acknowledge a weed management response is required immediately following a disaster before weeds spread beyond containment and create negative post-disaster outcomes
  • Prioritise inclusion of weed management funding in post-disaster grants available to Councils; preferably under Disaster Recovery Funding Arrangements (DRFA)
 
Background information
Weeds, along with loss of habitat and feral or pest animals, are known to be the major contributors to species loss.  Weeds such as Parramatta Grass and Giant Devil’s Fig are also causing major impacts to agricultural production.
 
The recent fire and flood disasters across the state have greatly exacerbated the spreading of weeds.  Floods spread weeds down rivers and creeks and across flood plains.  Bush fires remove native vegetation and at the same time open up vegetated areas to increased light which frequently results in major weed invasion.
 
At the recent Weeds NSW Conference, Dr. Marion Healy, Independent Biosecurity Commissioner of NSW, placed weeds among the significant climate change risks accompanying extreme weather.
 
We urgently need a forward response plan to minimise this negative post- disaster outcome.

 

The Motion was Carried 

VOTE FOR - Cr Chris Cherry (Mayor), Cr Meredith Dennis (Deputy Mayor), Cr Nola Firth, Cr Kimberly Hone
VOTE AGAINST - Cr Rhiannon Brinsmead, Cr James Owen
ABSENT. DID NOT VOTE -   Cr Reece Byrnes

Cr James Owen returned to the meeting at 06:21pm.

Cr Nola Firth
Cr Meredith Dennis (Deputy Mayor)

RESOLVED that Council:

  1. Notes that artificial lighting pollution is now known to cause potential ecological harm to wildlife including on migration navigation, immune response, mating, nesting, sleep patterns and rest, foraging habits, predator exposure, extent of roadkill, predator success and prevalence of invasive species. 

  2. Notes the wildlife friendly lighting guidelines from the National Light Pollution Guidelines for Wildlife (May 2023) including:
    1. Start with natural darkness and only adding light for specific purposes.
    2. Use adaptive light controls to manage light timing, intensity and colour.
    3. Lighting only the object or area intended – keep lights close to the ground, directed, and shielded to avoid light spill.
    4. Use the lowest intensity lighting appropriate for the task.
    5. Use non-reflective, dark-coloured surfaces.
    6. Use lights with reduced or filtered blue, violet and ultraviolet wavelengths.

  3. Notes that section 4.11 (Lighting Design) of the draft Tweed Development Control Plan 2025 (DCP) seeks to mitigate the effects of artificial light on wildlife and ecosystems by establishing design controls:
    1. for the lighting of roads and other public spaces in accordance with Australian Standard AS/NZS 1158 (2020) Lighting for Roads and Public Spaces
    2. for the lighting of playing / sports fields in accordance with Australian Standard AS 2560 (2018) Sports Lighting General Principles
    3. with consideration for the National Light Pollution Guidelines for Wildlife best practice lighting design

  4. Requests the General Manager to undertake a gap analysis on Council’s current lighting design standards against the National Light Pollution Guidelines for Wildlife best practice lighting design for Council managed parks and open space.
     
  5. Requests the General Manager to report to Council on the outcome of part 3 including the associated benefits, implications and costs of the potential changes.

  6. Uses its website, media and social networking channels to advise the community of the wildlife friendly lighting guidelines and the benefits and possible methods of installing it.
 

The Motion was Carried 

VOTE FOR - Cr Chris Cherry (Mayor), Cr Meredith Dennis (Deputy Mayor), Cr Rhiannon Brinsmead, Cr Nola Firth, Cr Kimberly Hone, Cr James Owen
VOTE AGAINST - None
ABSENT. DID NOT VOTE -   Cr Reece Byrnes

Cr Kimberly Hone
Cr Rhiannon Brinsmead

RESOLVED that the Councillor Expenses and Facilities Policy Version 4.0 be amended as follows:

  1. Information and communications technology (ICT) expenses - clause 6.42
    Council offers all Councillors standard ICT devices, being a Windows based laptop and an (optional) Apple iPad with keyboard, mouse and pen accessory. A Council issued mobile phone or a monthly allowance towards a handset cost. Councillor mobiles are to be equipped to access the internet on a plan. Council content on personal phones are subject to the State Records Act and Government Information Public Access Act and must be secured to Council standard when access Council's Wi-Fi is requested.

  2. Conferences and seminars - clause 6.36
    Costs associated with conference and seminars are covered by each individual Councillor's professional development budget annually (or for council term) to facilitate Councillor attendance at conferences and seminars. This allocation is for all Councillors. The General Manager will ensure that access to expenses relating to conferences and seminars is distributed equitably through the development of a Councillor Professional Development Plan which will have a bi-annual review mechanism. Once a Councillor's Professional Development budget is expended for the term, no further attendance at conference or seminars funded through the Councillors Professional Development Plan will be permitted for that term.

  3. Attendance at dinners and other non-Council functions - clause 6.50
    Before a Councillor attends a dinner or other non-Council function for which expenditure is significant (greater than $100) the Councillor must gain a Council resolution. Less than significant expenditure on dinners and non-Council functions may be authorised by the Public Officer and Director Corporate Services.

  4. Facilities - clause 9.1
    Council will provide the following facilities to Councillors to assist them to effectively discharge their civic duties:
    • a Councillor common room appropriately furnished and appropriate refreshments at both the Tweed Heads and Murwillumbah Civic Centres.

  5. Facilities - clause 9.2
    Councillors may book meeting rooms for official business in a specified Council building at no cost. Rooms may be booked through a specified officer in the Mayor's office (Personal Assistant to the Mayor & Councillors) or other specified staff member. Additionally, a room will be made available for Councillor only bookings at the Murwillumbah and Tweed offices and can be booked electronically by Councillors through the Councillor Portal or by contacting the Personal Assistant to Mayor & Councillors, on a first come, first served basis. Access to this room will be during business hours only and must sit outside of staff common or work areas. Use of the room is for Council related business only.

  6. Stationery and protective clothing - clause 9.4
    Council will provide the following stationery to Councillors each year:
    • letterhead, to be used for correspondence associated with civic duties
    • business cards. As an environmental initiative, Councillors can elect to have an e-business card that will be issued once. Once a Councillor has opted in to the e-business card, traditional business cards will no longer be issued.

  7. Appendix I: Monetary amounts

[IGNORE_INDENT]","reportContent":null,"minutesDiscussion":"Councillor Brinsmead asks could the Planning Unit use myLot (AI) to 'instantly answer planning enquiries and free up the team for higher value work'?

The Director Planning and Regulation replied:  Your suggestion regarding the potential use of “MyLot” AI to respond quickly to planning enquiries to free up the team for higher-value work.
MyLot” is one of several private AI products currently available on the market. Some products are designed as a customer-facing Q&A interface, while others focus on assessment assistance for staff. I have personally been a member of the My Lot AI Reference Group for several years and been offering feedback on how the product could be improved. Council has been keeping an active review of all AI products including Daisy being a digital planning assistant which has been implemented at Cumberland City Council and Wingecaribee Shire Council. We are also critically reviewing the Department of Plannings use of AI as Council’s often have to feed into the Departments system and synergies would be desirable. The Department of Planning have an AI solutions panel supplier list that includes:
  • Adaptovate Consulting using Daisy;
  • Archistar Platform
  • PropCode Trading using PropCode CDC
  • Sienna Planning using My Lot
While these systems all offer promise, they all require a very high level of setup and configuration, which is particularly challenging in NSW due to the complexity of planning legislation. Implementation involves significant backend work to ensure accuracy, compliance, and system integration. At present, the Council’s resources are focused on the YABBRU project, leaving limited capacity for the rollout of new AI solutions.
AI will certainly form part of the Planning & Regulation Unit’s future; however, we must be strategic in choosing the right tools at the right time to ensure they deliver value, are cost-effective, and enhance the customer experience. Any AI implementation should be approached as a whole-of-Council initiative to ensure affordability, effectiveness, and the best customer experience possible.","isPublic":false,"isPublished":false,"isCurrentItem":false,"meeting":null,"reports":[{"id":23099,"name":"Question With Notice","isUploaded":0,"reportTemplateId":18,"wordTemplateId":8,"pdfMediaFullPath":"stream/TWEED/tmp_24e8e52ed4.pdf","token":"b45efe09-8f4e-447d-846d-f2eb7840f9a8","isPublic":false}],"attachments":[],"actionSheets":[],"bookmarks":[{"id":3337,"name":"33","eventId":1650,"title":"QWN - Cr Brinsmead - myLot (AI)","text":"QWN - Cr Brinsmead - myLot (AI)","startTime":12930,"duration":null,"itemId":28504,"sortOrder":34,"minutesSortOrder":34,"parentId":-1,"additionalParentId":-1}],"minutes":[]},{"id":28505,"name":"QWN - Cr Brinsmead - Former Tweed Visitor Centre","parentId":27092,"sortOrder":66,"minutesSortOrder":65,"minutesParentId":27092,"outlineNumber":"2","fullOutlineNumber":"20.2.","htmlContent":"

[IGNORE_INDENT]","reportContent":null,"minutesDiscussion":"Councillor Brinsmead asks what can be done / had been done / will be done to assist Possums Community Preschool find a permanent home following their displacement from the Condong site as a result of the 2022 flood event?

Director Sustainable Communities and Environment replied:  Since the 2022 flood event, Council has provided ongoing support to Possums Community Preschool to help secure a permanent home following their displacement from the Condong site.

What has been done:
Without detailing every item, the following summarises the key points;
  • In September 2022 staff escalated the issue to Councillors and engaged early with the Department of Education regarding Condong Public School rebuild and potential co-location opportunities
  • Between January and March 2023 staff confirmed Council’s position that rebuilding at Condong was not feasible due to flood risk, while offering advocacy support with the Department of Education 
  • In March 2023 staff held multiple meetings with the Pre School to explore alternatives, including Murwillumbah South Infants School, co-location options, and potential land sites within the Murwillumbah area
  • In January 2024 staff assisted with transition planning, including the offer of salvaging and storage of equipment, and finalisation of the demolition of the flood-damaged Condong site.
  • From 2022 Council has provided letters of support, facilitated advocacy with local members of parliament, the Department of Education and the NSW Reconstruction Authority, and investigated alternative land and zoning options. More recently, Council advocated for a permanent site for the Pre School at the recent Community Cabinet meeting in Tweed Heads, and 
  • In July 2025 the General Manager connected the Pre School and a local real estate agent to a private property on the market that would likely meet the Pre School’s needs, and also identified alternate sites that may be of interest for them to investigate.
What is ongoing:
  • Council continues to liaise with the Department of Education, NSW Reconstruction Authority and other stakeholders to advocate for a long-term solution.
  • Ongoing discussions with the Pre School regarding interim options while they remain at Murwillumbah South Infants School where the lease has been extended to 2026
  • Continued support for advocacy towards a permanent solution, including land purchase opportunities, grant funding, and planning advice.
What can be done going forward:
  • Assist the Pre School in identifying and securing suitable interim premises to ensure continuity of service beyond the Murwillumbah South Infants School lease period.
  • Continue advocacy with State Government and relevant agencies to support the Pre School’s long-term goal of establishing a permanent home in Murwillumbah.
  • Provide planning advice and assistance with development approvals if a permanent site is secured.
  • Maintain regular communication and practical support to minimise disruption to preschool operations.

Cr Rhiannon Brinsmead
Cr Kimberly Hone

RESOLVED that:

1. The Minutes of the Local Traffic Committee Meeting held Thursday 10 July 2025 be received and 

2. The Executive Leadership Team's recommendations be adopted as follows:

6.1.    Queensland Road, Murwillumbah 
That the proposed temporary street closure at Queensland Road, Murwillumbah, for the Tweed Regional Museum Street Party, is approved on Saturday 6 September 2025 subject to: 
  1. Conformance with a Traffic Management Plan and associated Traffic Control Plans (submitted to Council at least 2 weeks before the event) implemented and controlled by Transport for NSW accredited persons.
  2. Community and affected business consultation addressing raised concerns including a letterbox drop to directly affected residents.
  3. All signage erected for the event to not cause a hazard for motorists or pedestrians and be removed immediately following the completion of the event.
  4. Consultation with emergency services and any identified issues addressed.
  5. Arrangements made for private property access and egress affected by the event.
  6. The submission and approval of a Community Event application/Major Event application and compliance with any conditions imposed therein.
  7. The event organiser is to ensure that any proposed roads or pathways used for the event have been assessed and are fit for purpose.
  8. No markings of any kind are to be used on road pavements as these markings can be a distraction to drivers.

7.1.    Drift Court, Kingscliff
The installation of prohibitive parking on Drift Court, Kingscliff is not supported given it a residential street with low traffic volumes. The request for parking enforcement has been forwarded onto Council’s Rangers.

7.2.    Eucalyptus Drive, Banora Point
Further advice on the provision of accessible parking facilities on the School land will be sought through the State Member's office (Geoff Provest MP) and will be provided back to this committee through Business Arising. 

7.3.    Henry Lawson Drive, Terranora
In relation to pedestrian crossing facilities on Henry Lawson Drive, Terranora, Council's preferred design and feedback are to be shared with Terranora Primary School and further support the school with safety messaging for parents and students. Additional pedestrian advisory signage can be investigated for installation in the interim of design construction, and Transport for NSW investigates opportunities to install flashing school zone lights.

7.4.    Twin Towns Triathlon Club, Triathlon Events 2025-2026
That the proposed Twin Towns Triathlon Club scheduled events beginning 27 September 2025 and concluding on 25 March 2026 be supported, subject to the following conditions:
  1. Adequate public liability insurance being held by the event organiser.
  2. All signage erected for the event to not cause a hazard for motorists or pedestrians and be removed immediately following the completion of the event.
  3. The event organiser is to ensure that any proposed roads or pathways used for the event have been assessed and are fit for purpose.
  4. Police approval be sought for the proposed bicycle race.

7.5.    McAllisters Road, Bilambil Heights 
That in relation to McAllisters Road, Bilambil Heights, Officers are to investigate physical means to reduce driver approach speeds to the north bound slip lane. It would be expected that the roundabout and intersection would be upgraded to accommodate future traffic generation associated with residential land release. 

The Motion was Carried 

VOTE FOR - Cr Chris Cherry (Mayor), Cr Meredith Dennis (Deputy Mayor), Cr Rhiannon Brinsmead, Cr Nola Firth, Cr Kimberly Hone, Cr James Owen
VOTE AGAINST - None
ABSENT. DID NOT VOTE -   Cr Reece Byrnes

[IGNORE_INDENT]","reportContent":null,"minutesDiscussion":"ALTERNATE MOTION

Cr Chris Cherry (Mayor)
Cr Nola Firth

RESOLVED that Council:
 
  1. Notes that without additional resourcing, the capacity to actively engage in local food system development and food security initiatives is limited.

  2. Continues to promote local food system opportunities, support growers and participate in initiatives as staff and resourcing allow.

  3. Continues to engage with the Rural Land Industry Management Committee to pursue local food system initiatives that contribute to food security.

  4. Resolves that questions about food security are incorporated in the next Community Strategic Plan engagement process to capture lived experience and community sentiment.

  5. Writes to NSW DPI-Agriculture and provides them with the relevant feedback provided by the Rural Advisory Committee with regards to food security, requesting their help with implementation including: 

    1. Facilitate incubator and lease arrangements for farmers to farm prime agricultural land, and make land available for urban agriculture, including underutilised Crown land. 
    2. Streamline agribusiness development applications including on-farm sale points and processing  (i.e. butchering). 
    3. Conduct consultation with local farm businesses to identify challenges and impediments to the survival and success of their enterprise and identify actions that Council can take to assist their farm business. 
    4. Conduct bi-annual workshops conducted to provide the sector with ideas on how to improve their food security and resilience. 
    5. Fund a pilot sponsorship program for farmers to lease land and/or build business skills to maintain a regenerative farm business. 
    6. Maintain the Profitable Regenerative Farming Program (current Environmental Trust-funded project to help farmers develop business skills in regenerative agriculture) to connect local mentors to new farm businesses. 
    7. Support small-scale and large-scale producers through initiatives that recognise the value of their businesses for local food security (i.e. providing signage similar to Land for Wildlife to recognize Tweed Valley producers, certificate of recognition or certification schemes). 

  6. Engages with Hort Innovation to obtain information and ideas about what grows best here, and technological innovations that reduce the cost of labour and inputs. Sustainable Agriculture staff to participate in a future Hort Innovation food conference to gather information.

  7. Includes preference for regionally produced foods and locally owned food business in our update of Councils procurement policy.
 

The Motion was Carried 

VOTE FOR - Cr Chris Cherry (Mayor), Cr Meredith Dennis (Deputy Mayor), Cr Rhiannon Brinsmead, Cr Nola Firth, Cr Kimberly Hone, Cr James Owen
VOTE AGAINST - None
ABSENT. DID NOT VOTE -   Cr Reece Byrnes

Naomi Searle - Director Sustainable Communities and Environment declared a Non-Pecuniary, non-significant Interest in Item 13.2 - Major Project United Kingscliff Redevelopment. The nature of the interest is that Director Searle owns a property adjacent to the site. Director Searle will manage the Interest by remaining in the Chamber for discussion and acting impartially.

ALTERNATE MOTION

Cr Chris Cherry (Mayor)
Cr Nola Firth

RESOLVED that Council endorses the wording of the Draft Submission dated 4 August 2024 to the Department of Planning, Housing & Industry for the proposed Uniting Kingscliff Redevelopment (SSD-47105958) which is to be forwarded to the Department as a final submission. That Council endorses the wording of the Draft Submission dated 4 August 2024, with the following additional text:
 
  1.  Add the following sentence (in red) into the report at 4a as follows: 

    4a. It is recommended that balustrades on units that are oriented to the external boundaries should be designed to limit overlooking of existing residential development. "It is noted that the use of a single rather than double corridor to address overlooking was an earlier design commitment to residents that has not been included." Opaque glass or other visually non-permeable materials is recommended. 

  2. "Council highlights the submission from the SES as the main body legislatively tasked in NSW with responsibility for flood rescue, these points from the SES submission on this development should be particularly noted: 

    • This proposal is likely to result in a significantly increased requirement for government spending on emergency management services, flood mitigation and emergency response measures, particularly given the vulnerability of the occupants. 
    • There are considerable risks associated with evacuating aged care residents, particularly those requiring specialised medical care and equipment, as acknowledged in the FERP. Similarly, there are considerable risks associated with extremely vulnerable people sheltering in buildings surrounded by floodwaters who may be isolated for more than 50 hours, and potentially up to 3 days. 
    • The change in flood probabilities with climate change for this catchment area results in the new probability of the 1 in 100 AEP to be approximately 1 in 62 AEP event for the current 2025 scenario, becoming even more frequent in the future. For the proposed development site, this could result in more frequent inundation and isolation than what is currently expected based on previous modelling. 
    • It is noted that all proposed buildings will have their ground floor level, which is intended for  habitable uses, at 3.8m AHD, which is above the 1% AEP flood level, with over-floor flooding  expected between the 1% AEP and the 0.2% AEP event - flooding of all ground floor levels of  around 0.7 metres depth is expected in the 0.2% AEP event*.
    • While we understand that the proposal replaces an existing single storey aged care facility  with a finished floor level of approximately 3.57m AHD, (capacity of 171 people, with no opportunity to shelter in place in a flood event) with a larger, multi-storey complex (with a  capacity of 424 people, with space above the PMF for residents to shelter in place), the  existing risk should not be used to justify increasing the number of vulnerable people in a  high-risk floodplain by relying on shelter in place (SIP) as “the primary flood emergency response strategy for the majority of the RAC residents and the back-up strategy for the rest of the site occupants. 
    • The 'shelter in place' strategy is not an endorsed flood management strategy by the NSW SES  for future development. Such an approach is only considered suitable for existing dwellings where the risk of staying is lower than the risk of evacuating, without increasing the number  of people subject to such risk/s. 
    • DPE (2022) recommends SIP can be used if the duration of flood inundation is less than 6  hours. The site may be isolated for up to 50 hours. Therefore, according to the NSW  Department of Planning and Environment (DPE) shelter-in-place guideline (2022), shelter in place is not a recommended flood emergency response strategy for the proposed development.
    • Sheltering in place is especially dangerous considering the site is a Low Flood Island (people can get trapped at the site on the top floors) and the proposal is for sensitive development, with many residents requiring specialised medical care and essential equipment (such as continuous oxygen). We would like to emphasise that these are extremely vulnerable people.  
    • We recommend progressively relocating such vulnerable development outside of the floodplain, as recommended by the Flood Inquiry2022. 

      *Council notes that the proposal has been amended to have a ground floor level of 4.1m since the SES submission was received.

      Council also advises the Department that Councils Floodplain Management Advisory Committee advised in December 2024 that it recommends adopting the higher level obtained from the 2024 Tweed Valley Flood Study Update and Expansion 1% AEP Level, the 2009 Tweed Valley Flood Study 1% AEP Level or the “Flood of Record” Level (i.e. 2017 or 2022), plus an allowance for climate change as the Interim Flood Planning Levels for Tweed Shire. Please take this community’s and SES’s concerns re flood safety into consideration when assessing this proposal."

 

The Motion was Carried 

VOTE FOR - Cr Chris Cherry (Mayor), Cr Meredith Dennis (Deputy Mayor), Cr Rhiannon Brinsmead, Cr Nola Firth, Cr Kimberly Hone, Cr James Owen
VOTE AGAINST - None
ABSENT. DID NOT VOTE -   Cr Reece Byrnes

Director Sustainable, Communities and Environment replied:  Illegal camping and animal control patrols are currently conducted throughout the week including weekends at locations across the Tweed.  Locations are selected each week based on customer service requests, reports from operational crews and field observations.   Current focus areas over the past two months have included high-value community assets such as Jack Evans Boat Harbour, and open spaces or sporting fields experiencing high visitation numbers or scheduled events such as the Walter Peate Reserve during school-age athletics carnivals.
 
In addition to these ordinary patrols, weekly public space patrols have been conducted in conjunction with NSW Police officers since the end of June. The locations for these patrols are selected by Council Rangers on the basis of field observations regarding anti-social behaviour and customer service requests.  Locations are also identified by the Police based on their field observations and reports received.  Primary locations have been JEBH (and Coral Street), Chris Cunningham Park, and Keith Compton Drive (Island Drive, Frances Street, Bay Street, Brett Street).  This has resulted in a number of people being referred to Assertive Outreach, a number of illegal camps being dismantled and taken away, and people who are being anti-social being moved on.  These patrols will continue through the spring months.
 
Joint targeted illegal camping and animal control patrols are also undertaken out of hours with NSW Police on a periodic basis.  These targeted patrols will continue during peak periods, primarily during school holidays as resources allow.  This is in addition to Rangers undertaking their regular patrols.

CONFIDENTIAL COMMITTEE

REPRESENTATIONS FOR ITEMS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE
(Sec 3.40, 13.9 to 13.17 Model Code of Meeting Practice)
 
Under Council’s Model Code of Meeting Practice, members of the public may make representations before any part of the meeting is closed to the public, as to whether that part of the meeting should be closed.  If you wish to make any representations, you are invited to do so now.
 
EXCLUSION OF PRESS AND PUBLIC

Cr Meredith Dennis (Deputy Mayor) 
Cr James Owen
   
RESOLVED that Council moves itself into a Confidential Committee in accordance with Section 10A(2) of the Local Government Act 1993 and that the press and public be excluded from the whole of the Committee Meeting, because, in the opinion of the Committee, publicity of the proceedings of the Committee would be prejudicial to the public interest, by reasons of the confidential nature of the business to be transacted.   
   
The Motion was Carried

VOTE FOR - Cr Chris Cherry (Mayor), Cr Meredith Dennis (Deputy Mayor), Cr Rhiannon Brinsmead, Cr Reece Byrnes, Cr Kimberly Hone, Cr James Owen
VOTE AGAINST - None
ABSENT. DID NOT VOTE - Cr Nola Firth

The meeting opened with a Prayer read by Pastor Rob Stuttle from the Living Waters Church, Tumbulgum:

"As Father’s Day is approaching, I’ll read a summary of a prayer in Daniel Chapter 9, modified for our Shire:

Our awesome Father God, the Covenant keeping God, with unfailing love, who keeps his promises. We as a nation have sinned and not walked according to your instruction or in a way that is worthy of the love you have towards us. 

You have been merciful towards us even when we have rebelled against you.

Your love and patience is so evident even when we don’t deserve it.

You proved it when you rescued your people from the Egyptians when they didn’t deserve it.

Lord hear our prayer today that we may turn and seek your face. That we acknowledge that this amazing land we live in is a gift from God, and you are the one who causes the sun to shine and the rain to fall.

We ask for our mercy and help for every Councillor here today as they preside over matters relating to Tweed Shire Council.

We ask this in Jesus name
Amen"
